name: Zinc lozenges

lead: Zinc lozenges are dissolving tablets of a zinc salt, mainly sold for colds. Some people also use them for breath, reasoning that zinc binds the smelly sulfur compounds behind bad breath.

For colds, the proposed mechanism is zinc acting locally in the throat, and lab work has examined zinc salts against rhinoviruses. Randomized trials since 1984 have reported mixed results on cold duration. No lozenge trial in the sources reviewed tested breath; the breath rationale is the binding of sulfur compounds seen with zinc in rinses.

paras: They are dissolved slowly in the mouth, typically in the early days of a cold. Breath-focused users take them in the same way, often alongside other oral-care steps.
Trials report bad taste and mouth irritation. Zinc nasal products were linked to loss of smell and drew an FDA warning in 2009, which did not cover oral lozenges.

angle.text: Zinc lozenges are best known as a cold remedy, and some oral-care users also take them hoping zinc neutralises the sulfur compounds behind bad breath. Trials have studied them for colds, with mixed results, and not for breath.

lead: Zinc lozenges are dissolvable tablets containing a zinc salt, most often zinc gluconate or zinc acetate. They are best known as a common cold remedy, and some people in oral-care circles also use them in the belief that zinc neutralizes the sulfur compounds behind bad breath.[1][2]

The cold literature is large: randomized trials since 1984 have tested zinc lozenges, with some reporting shorter cold duration and others reporting no benefit, and reviews describe mixed results.[2][3][4] No trial in the sources reviewed here tests zinc lozenges for breath or other appearance outcomes; a registered trial comparing probiotic with zinc-chlorhexidine mouthwash for halitosis in orthodontic patients involves a different product.[5]

paras: The main studied use is shortening common colds. A 1984 double-blind trial of 23 mg zinc gluconate lozenges reported 86% of 37 zinc-treated subjects asymptomatic after seven days versus 46% of 28 placebo subjects, with side effects mostly limited to objectionable taste and mouth irritation.[6] The use for breath is a community belief; the proposed rationale is that zinc ions bind volatile sulfur compounds, and no lozenge trial in the sources examined measured this.

Early trials describe taste complaints and mouth irritation.[6] Wikipedia notes that intranasal zinc products, which are a different dosage form, were linked to loss of smell, and the FDA in 2009 warned consumers about three Zicam nasal products; that warning did not cover oral lozenges.[7]

A 2000 randomized trial of 50 people found zinc acetate lozenges associated with shorter cold duration.[1] A 1998 JAMA trial in children and adolescents tested zinc gluconate glycine lozenges.[8] The 2013 Cochrane review described the trials since 1984 as having mixed results and noted that inadequate masking and reduced zinc bioavailability in some formulations may have influenced them.[3] A 2017 meta-analysis compared zinc acetate with zinc gluconate and examined the role of dosage.[2] No study in the sources reviewed tested zinc lozenges for halitosis.
